title: The Difference Between False And Worthy Praise
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin responds to reader pushback on a prior article by drawing a sharp line between false praise and worthy praise. False praise, he argues, is given to manipulate students through public compliments for merely expected behavior, and it benefits the teacher rather than the student. Worthy praise, by contrast, is honest feedback grounded in genuine accomplishment beyond what a student has previously done, delivered quietly and only after work is complete. He contends that false praise produces short-term compliance but erodes intrinsic motivation and confuses students about what excellence actually looks like. Worthy praise, though sometimes as subtle as a nod or a fist bump, builds real motivation and a truthful sense of ability. The piece closes with an appeal to hold students to a higher, more honest standard of feedback.
points: Distinguishes false praise (manipulative, given for expected behavior, benefits the teacher) from worthy praise (honest, earned, benefits the student).
Argues false praise lowers the bar for what counts as excellent and can inflate students' sense of their own abilities.
Recommends a simple 'Thank you' rather than false praise when students merely meet an expectation.
Worthy praise should arrive only after work is completed and can be as subtle as a nod or fist bump.
Frames the argument as grounded in three decades of testing strategies with thousands of teachers, not a bid for controversy.
quotes: False praise is praise given in order to appease, flatter, or manipulate students into doing what the teacher wants. In other words, it isn’t based on genuine accomplishment.
The beneficiary of false praise is the teacher, not the students.
So what should you say after your students complete an expectation as taught? “Thank you” will do.

Worthy praise is praise based on true accomplishment, which can be defined as new learning or effort or performance beyond what is commonly expected or what an individual student or group has done before.
The actual moment of praise may be subtle. It may be a nod from across the room or a silent fist bump. But its power to motivate and inspire students to seek taller mountains to climb has no bounds.
My firm stance on praise isn’t for the purpose of clickbait. I’m not trying to be controversial.
